title: What options exist for running AEO without a large team?
content:
Companies without the internal resources or budget to build a dedicated search department still need to know what options exist for running AEO without a large team. Answer Engine Optimization is no longer optional for companies that rely on search to generate leads and revenue. AI Overviews now appear at the top of search results before a single organic listing — and sometimes above paid ads.
Three paths exist for running AEO without a large team. The first is a DIY workflow built around free or low-cost tools. The second is a complete software solution like HubSpot AEO that centralizes tracking and recommendations. The third is agency support for teams that want the work handled externally.
The right path depends on how much time the team can dedicate each week, what budget is available, and how consistently measurement can be turned into action. This article covers each path, walks through a minimum viable workflow for getting started, and provides starter prompts for building a repeatable tracking system.
Answer Engine Optimization requires measurement, prompt tracking, and content updates. All three can start in a single week without a dedicated specialist.
Four foundational elements determine how well AEO runs on a lean team. Each one is covered below, along with how AI tools can handle the execution work without adding headcount.
The baseline visibility check comes first. It establishes where the brand currently stands in AI-generated answers before any strategy work begins. A useful baseline covers three things: whether the brand is mentioned at all, how it is described when it appears, and which competitors show up in its place. Without this starting point, teams have no way to measure whether later efforts actually work.
Two affordable approaches exist for getting a baseline:
AI Search Grader is built for marketers who need a starting point without committing time or budget upfront. AI Search Grader requires no setup, no integration, and no dedicated tool spend. For a lean team, the value is speed — a marketer gets an initial read on brand visibility fast enough to fold into an existing workday, then uses that starting point to decide what comes next.
AI Search Grader organizes brand performance into five categories.
AI Search Grader gives marketers a one-time visibility snapshot. HubSpot AEO supports ongoing tracking, which makes AI Search Grader a useful starting point for teams not yet ready to commit to a full monitoring workflow. To get the most complete picture, combining AI Search Grader with a round of manual prompts covers both the structured score and the raw search behavior.
A starter prompt set should include 15 to 20 prompts, organized into four categories.
Mixing all four matters because buyers rarely start with a brand name. Non-brand searches are where AEO needs to focus its efforts. Over 30% of Gen Zers find information through chatbots or AI, and 47% of today’s marketers use AI for research, according to HubSpot’s AI Trends for Marketers report . A prompt set built entirely from branded questions will show strong visibility that does not reflect how the brand actually performs when a buyer is comparing options.
Here are some examples of prompts and the categories they belong to.
One important caveat: AI search results are personalized. Results vary based on a user’s location, account history, and device, so what one marketer sees when testing a prompt will not always match what an actual buyer sees. That variability is worth factoring in when interpreting baseline results.
Phrasing also matters more in AI search than in traditional search. Two closely related prompts — “best CRM for small teams” and “best CRM for a five-person sales team” — can return different answers. Answer engines respond to the specific phrasing of a question rather than matching intent against a broader set of related terms the way traditional search does.
Because phrasing matters more in AI search than in traditional search, a manual prompt set, however well built, is a snapshot rather than a fully reliable measure, and it will not catch every variation a real buyer might search. Tracking is better managed with tools, but we’ll get onto that later.
Pro tip: Once the set is locked in and the first visibility test has been run, it becomes the fixed benchmark the team tracks over time. Keeping the prompt set consistent from week to week is what makes comparisons meaningful.
A starter prompt set only earns its keep if someone actually looks at the results. Regular review is what turns visibility data into next steps for the marketing team.
Three things are worth watching for in each review:
A weekly review does not have to mean manually re-checking everything. Teams using AI tools can speed up workflows like this and shrink reporting time significantly.
Tracking AEO performance without acting on it will not move visibility. Answer engines draw from sources beyond a brand’s website, including third-party articles, forums, reviews, and social content. An ongoing content plan is what turns tracking data into actual visibility gains.
Recency matters more than most teams expect. Content published within the last five years accounts for 94% of LLM crawler hits, according to a study from Seer Interactive , with most of that share going to content published in just the past year. An old blog post that once ranked well will not keep earning citations on reputation alone. When the data, examples, or statistics inside it go stale, answer engines look elsewhere for something more current to cite.
Because recency matters more than most teams expect, publishing and updating are two separate, ongoing activities.
Recency does not carry equal weight across every industry, and that difference should shape how often an update cycle runs. The same Seer Interactive study found three distinct patterns.
A single update cycle will not serve every brand equally. The right cadence depends on how quickly the topics a brand covers tend to change.
Pro tip: Content updates made for AEO do not need to happen in isolation from existing SEO work. Marketing Hub SEO software surfaces prioritized recommendations to fix on-site issues, identifies topic clusters to build search authority, and integrates keyword data with Google Search Console. Strengthening topic authority through this kind of tool supports the same content answer engines are more likely to cite, since both traditional search and AI search reward clear, well-structured, authoritative content.
Lean marketing teams can run Answer Engine Optimization with one to three people, provided they choose the right setup, from DIY, software, and/or agency support. The right option depends on how effort, cost, control, and speed weigh against each other.
The comparison below covers effort, cost, control, and speed for each path.
DIY costs the least in dollars but the most in time. A marketer manually testing prompts, logging results in a spreadsheet, and cross-referencing SEO data has full control over the process. The approach scales poorly past a handful of prompts and tends to fall apart the first time the team gets busy. It works best as a starting point, not a long-term system.
The learning curve is steeper than most teams expect. AEO is a newer discipline than SEO, the industry is full of conflicting advice, and there is no equivalent decade of established playbooks to lean on. A marketer starting from scratch needs to research how answer engines work, figure out which platforms matter most for the audience, and build a working process before any tracking even begins.
Using an agency removes the time burden but comes with less day-to-day control and a higher price point. External teams can run AEO monitoring and content recommendations without pulling internal bandwidth, which suits companies with budget but no internal capacity.
The tradeoff is speed. Insights or content support often has to pass through the internal team before work can proceed. A nuance an in-house marketer would catch instantly can take a full reporting cycle to surface and correct when routed through an external agency partner.
Cost is the other factor. Agency retainers for AEO work vary widely, and pricing models are still inconsistent across providers since the discipline is relatively new. Agency support tends to make the most sense for teams with the budget to fully outsource AEO — not for teams looking to supplement limited internal capacity, since the cost only pays off when there is enough spend to make full outsourcing worthwhile.
Pro tip: The strongest agency candidates are those with a search marketing background, such as an SEO agency that has expanded into AEO. The two disciplines share enough overlap in content quality, structured data, and authority signals that an agency already familiar with the brand’s SEO performance has a meaningful head start.
Software sits between the two other paths and works best for most lean teams. For a team weighing options, software is where an AEO strategy pays off fastest.
HubSpot AEO helps marketers track brand visibility, competitor presence, citations, and recommendations across answer engines. It centralizes the same tracking work a DIY spreadsheet would require, without the manual overhead or the agency price tag.
A one-person marketing team benefits from this setup more than a larger team does, since there is no one else to absorb the tracking work if it slips. Prompts get set up once and run on a recurring basis rather than being rebuilt by hand each week. When results come in, they include a specific recommendation — a page to update or a gap to close — so the marketer is not left interpreting raw data without a clear next step.
For a marketer covering strategy, content, and reporting alone, automating prompt setup and providing specific recommendations is the difference between AEO being a sustainable part of the job and another task that quietly stops happening.
HubSpot AEO keeps measurement and content recommendations in one place, connected to the same platform many teams already use for SEO . That makes AEO an extension of existing workflows rather than a separate initiative to maintain.
For teams weighing all three paths, the deciding question is usually not which option is best in the abstract. It is which one the team will actually keep up with. A consolidated software option is usually the best choice for teams that need ongoing measurement without the complexity of an enterprise-grade system or the cost of full agency support.
Pro tip: For teams building out a lean marketing function more broadly, see HubSpot’s guide to how to build the strongest small marketing team .
A baseline visibility check can be completed in a single sitting. Pick a handful of prompts across ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews, and Perplexity, then note whether the brand shows up, how it is described, and which competitors appear instead. AI Search Grader handles a lot of that work in a single pass without manual prompt-by-prompt testing.
A one-time snapshot captures a single moment. It answers the question of where the brand stands right now, but not whether that position is getting better or worse. A brand could run a baseline, see a strong result, and have no way of knowing whether it holds up a month later.
Ongoing tracking closes that gap. The same prompts run on a regular cadence, results logged over time, and changes flagged as they happen rather than discovered weeks later. Ongoing tracking is where AEO tools for small teams become worth the investment. Manually repeating a baseline check every week is exactly the kind of task that stops happening once the team gets busy.
HubSpot AEO is built for this ongoing layer. It tracks brand visibility, competitor presence, and citations on a recurring basis. AEO in Marketing Hub Pro and Enterprise adds CRM-informed prompt suggestions and a tighter path from recommendations to action, so tracking data becomes a specific next step rather than a report that sits unread.
HubSpot AEO Sensor adds a layer a brand-specific tracker cannot provide on its own. This free dashboard tracks AI answer engine volatility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. It helps teams tell the difference between a market-wide shift and a gap specific to the brand’s own AEO work. The distinction between a market-wide shift and a gap specific to the brand’s AEO work matters for a lean team especially — chasing an industry-wide drop wastes time that could go toward fixing actual brand-specific gaps.
Together, a fast baseline and ongoing tracking answer two different questions. One shows where the brand stands today. The other shows whether that position is holding, improving, or slipping. A lean team does not need both running at full scale from day one, but understanding the difference keeps a one-time snapshot from being mistaken for a tracking system.
A fast baseline shows where a brand stands today. Ongoing tracking shows whether that position holds. What connects the two is a workflow — a fixed set of prompts tested the same way every time, so results mean something when compared week over week.
The starter prompt set covered earlier introduced four prompt categories. Below are five example prompts for each, ready to adapt to any brand or industry.
Category prompts test whether a brand shows up when a buyer hasn’t named it yet, which is often the clearest signal of how much work AEO actually needs.
Competitor prompts show share of voice directly, and they tend to surface gaps a brand’s own branded prompts never will.
These prompts move beyond the category level to specific scenarios a buyer might actually search for, testing whether a brand’s content maps to real use cases rather than just broad category terms.
Objection-style prompts test whether a brand’s content addresses real hesitations or leaves the field open for a competitor’s content to fill that gap instead.
A lean team can run a full manual workflow using free tools like AI Search Grader for a baseline and spreadsheet tracking for ongoing prompts. This approach trades lower upfront cost for higher ongoing time investment and lower consistency, since manual tracking is usually the first task to slip once a marketer gets busy.
Free tools like AI Search Grader can also cover the initial baseline step without any spend, which makes a no-tool start realistic for teams testing whether AEO is worth deeper investment before committing to a full AEO platform pilot.
There’s no fixed timeline for how long it takes to see changes in AI answers. Answer engines update at different rates depending on whether they pull from live web search or from training data. Weekly reviews matter more than a single before-and-after check, since gradual shifts are easy to miss without consistent tracking.
SEO and AI workflows should run alongside each other rather than compete for the same content resources. Strong SEO fundamentals like topic authority and clear content structure tend to support AEO performance too, so improving one often benefits the other.
An agency makes the most sense once there’s budget to fully outsource AEO rather than just supplement limited internal capacity, since agency costs only pay off at that scale. An SEO agency that has expanded into AEO tends to be a stronger fit than one treating AEO as an entirely new discipline requiring a separate retainer.
No. The baseline visibility check, prompt tracking, and most content updates can be handled by a marketer without any developer involvement.
Whatever path a team chooses, HubSpot AEO and supporting free tools like AI Search Grader and AI Search Sensor are worth adding into the mix. A DIY workflow is only as good as the time available to run it consistently. HubSpot AEO removes that dependency by tracking brand visibility, competitor presence, and citations automatically. For teams working with an agency, it provides an internal view of performance between reporting cycles rather than waiting on an external team to surface a shift already visible in the data.
For teams on Marketing Hub Pro or Enterprise, CRM-informed recommendations tie visibility data directly to a next action. That connects visibility data directly to action instead of creating another dashboard that goes unread.
